This study introduces a new approach to the semantic parsing challenge by integrating a syntax-based framework with the BERT model. The method employs BERT to extract semantic features from syntax trees, which are subsequently encoded to generate a fixed-size representation. This strategy offers two primary benefits: first, leveraging pre-trained BERT allows the system to capture deep semantic information, while relying on syntax ensures the extraction of rich structural features. Second, the resulting fixed-size representation facilitates the use of efficient, lightweight architectures. The approach was validated on the SemEval2018 task 1 dataset, specifically the WikiHow dataset, where it achieved state-of-the-art performance.

We have conducted a series of 3D general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations to investigate the jet-to-outflow ratio in neutrino-cooled accretion disks surrounding post-merger black holes. Our findings indicate that this ratio is highly dependent on the magnetic flux ratio at the disk's outer edge relative to its inner edge, which itself is governed by the initial configuration of the binary system. Specifically, when the magnetic flux ratio is low, the resulting outflow is bipolar, with the jet comprising a minor fraction of the total mass ejection. Conversely, a high magnetic flux ratio yields a mixed outflow where jets and outflows contain comparable mass. These observations align with previous studies on magnetized accretion disks, which demonstrated that a critical magnetic flux ratio exists that maximizes the mass in non-accreting components.

We introduce a novel method for quantifying the fractional flux contained within tidal structures of galaxies, validated through simulations of galaxy mergers. This technique was applied to 1,000 Early-Type Galaxies (ETGs) with masses exceeding $10^{10} M_\odot$ from the HSC-SSP sample, which were identified and classified using a convolutional neural network (CNN). Our findings indicate that the distribution of this fractional flux in tidal material follows a log-normal pattern, peaking around 1%. We detect tidal features in approximately 10% of galaxies with masses above $10^{11} M_\odot$, a proportion that declines for lower-mass ETGs. Leveraging these observations, we calculated the merger rate for ETGs in the HSC-SSP sample, estimating roughly 10% of galaxies above $10^{11} M_\odot$ have undergone a merger within the last 1.5 billion years. This rate decreases with mass, reaching about 1% for galaxies around $10^{10.5} M_\odot$. These results align with the observed frequency of tidal features and support a scenario where massive ETGs are the primary products of major mergers.

This study represents the second installment of a series exploring the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which posits that the Newtonian gravitational potential is modified by a logarithmic term. This modification stems from the requirement of a repulsive gravitational component to account for observed galactic rotation curves. Building on the first paper in this series, this article investigates the consequences of such a potential on star clusters and planetary systems. It is demonstrated that the repulsive gravity inherent in ASTG is sufficiently strong to generate bipolar outflows from these systems. These findings are compared with the current understanding of galactic outflows, and the implications of these results for the origin of bipolar outflows are discussed.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense radio signals, yet their origins remain unknown. While the collapsar model for long-duration gamma-ray bursts suggests FRBs might arise from similar mechanisms, such as the collapse of a massive star or the merger of compact objects, their much shorter durations have made direct optical counterparts elusive. This study reports the discovery of 100 fast radio bursts by CHIME, 20 of which were observed by the CHIME/FRB project. For these events, we conducted simultaneous and delayed optical searches using the Palomar Transient Factory-Rapid (PTF-R) instrument on the 1.5-m Samuel Oschin Telescope at Palomar Observatory. Our results place the most stringent limits to date on the occurrence rate of optical emission associated with FRBs. Specifically, we constrain the peak-to-average luminosity ratio to be less than 100 at 95% confidence and set an absolute upper limit on the peak optical luminosity of approximately $10^{35}$ erg s$^{-1}$. These findings rule out several proposed FRB progenitors, including the magnetospheric collapse of young neutron stars and the merger of compact objects.

This work details a methodology for modeling, designing, and refining laser beam propagation across gaseous laser mediums, specifically targeting high-power industrial systems. The research focuses on three interconnected areas: the modeling of laser interaction within the gas medium, the initial design of the laser geometry, and subsequent optimization or inverse design. The interaction model accounts for the coupled nonlinear Maxwell-Bloch equations, addressing key phenomena such as self-focusing, the nonlinear refractive index, and the dynamic evolution of the gas medium. The design methodology utilizes a gas discharge tube filled with the laser gas, excited by an external laser pump. The configuration is optimized to maximize extracted power by optimizing the spatial distribution of the pump laser. The optimization and inverse design processes rely on the adjoint method, which is integrated with deep neural networks to predict the pump laser distribution required to achieve a desired outcome. The study concludes by presenting a case study of the inverse design for a CO₂ gas laser system.

While GPT-2 and similar architectures excel at generating coherent text, they frequently lack the ability to produce visual descriptions. This limitation stems from the difficulty of integrating visual inputs into existing language models. This work introduces a novel method for controlling the visual output of pre-trained models by injecting learned visual embeddings directly into the self-attention layers of the encoder. This approach enables the generation of visual content without requiring fine-tuning or modifications to the language model's weights. We demonstrate that this framework is versatile, successfully supporting both generative and predictive tasks, and is validated through qualitative and quantitative evaluations on the visual description, image captioning, and machine translation domains.

This research introduces a modified ring signature scheme that streamlines the verification process to reduce the value of $k$, thereby enabling lighter anonymous transaction systems for cryptocurrencies. By shifting certain computational burdens from verifiers to signers through delegation, the system achieves a speed advantage. We demonstrate that this approach expands the practical limits of current digital money by supporting higher throughput and lower fees. The analysis includes a formal proof of security and validation of the system's resistance to various attacks. Finally, we provide implementation results showing a transaction verification process that is 100 times faster than that of Bitcoin.

This study outlines a systematic approach to beam luminosity scans, presenting data from recent scans conducted at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) during runs in 2018 and 2021. We analyze the resulting scans to derive key interaction point parameters, including beam separation, centroid movements, and the Luminosity Scanning Function (LSF) along with its LSF asymmetry. Furthermore, we examine the correlations linking these LSF characteristics to beam losses.

We illustrate this approach with a case study involving a cantilever beam subjected to a dynamic load, where we use a collaborative method to optimize the hyperparameters of both a physics-based and a data-driven model. This work examines $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays involving the $^3D_4$ $\Upsilon(10753)$ state using an $^3D_4$-$^1D_4$-$^5D_4$ coupled-channel framework to study the $^{1D_4}$ and $^{5D_4}$ $\Upsilon(10753)$ components. The calculated branching ratios for these processes are found to be negligibly small.

Training neural networks with reduced precision offers significant memory and computational advantages, yet it often results in degraded accuracy. We introduce a novel approach that combines quantization with optimization constraints to restore performance. The method, Ask SGD, utilizes a two-stage training process: the first stage employs a standard optimizer on floating-point parameters, while the second adapts these to a specific set of discrete weights using our proposed method. This second stage is further refined by incorporating momentum and handling asymmetric quantization levels. Experimental results demonstrate that Ask SGD achieves superior accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art techniques across various benchmarks.

Soft robotics is a rapidly developing field that offers significant potential for creating robots capable of interacting safely with humans and their environments. However, these systems are inherently complex due to their continuous configuration, nonlinear characteristics, dynamic behavior, and coupling effects. To address these complexities, research has increasingly turned toward simulation-based approaches. This paper provides a comprehensive review of modeling and simulation techniques for both the kinematics and dynamics of soft robots. We examine various approaches ranging from physics-based to data-driven methods, highlighting the advantages and constraints of each. Furthermore, we discuss advanced simulation-based control strategies, including model-based learning and hybrid approaches that integrate simulation with real-world data. Finally, we outline the challenges and future research directions within modeling, simulation, and control of soft robots.

This study examines the real Jacobi group, defined as the semi-direct product comprising $GL(2, \mathbb{R})$ and the space of real symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrices. We establish its Lie algebra and derive its representations by leveraging representations of the Weil algebra and the Fourier transform.

Verifying factual claims using tables is challenging because it demands the integration of multiple cognitive skills, such as cross-checking claim information against tables, discerning ambiguities in queries, and identifying contradictions. Although current models achieve reasonable results, they frequently err by attributing tabular discrepancies to the claims themselves rather than recognizing when tables and claims mismatch. To address this, we propose an approach leveraging task decomposition, which yields significant performance gains. Our method also demonstrates that splitting a problem into simpler, sequential sub-tasks enhances LLM effectiveness in verification tasks, provided each individual step is easy to solve.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are highly effective for synthesizing realistic images, though their non-differentiable nature prevents direct optimization within latent space, limiting their utility for data augmentation. This study introduces a method to derive differentiable latent representations, facilitating the integration of GANs into end-to-end training pipelines. We evaluate this approach on the CIFAR-10 dataset, demonstrating that our technique generates high-quality augmented data and supports conditioning for image synthesis.

Bayesian nested sampling (BNS) functions as a technique to determine evidence and characterize posteriors within high-dimensional spaces, particularly those constrained by non-analytical likelihoods. While recent advancements have proposed using slice sampling to transition BNS into an exact method, this paper introduces a novel approach utilizing truncated slice sampling. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of both variants against traditional sampler choices, focusing on containment in likelihood ridges and convergence rates across diverse scenarios. Results indicate that, in general, the proposed truncated version outperforms the original slice sampling and standard samplers. However, specific cases involving high-dimensional likelihood ridges favor traditional slice sampling, an observation corroborated by our analysis of the 3D Ising model.

The objective of fault-tolerant distance labeling is to map each vertex $u$ of a graph $G$ to a binary string $l(u)$ such that, for any vertex set $F$ with size at most $k$, the union of labels forms a code where the Hamming distance between $l(u)$ and $l(v)$ exactly equals the graph distance $d_G(u,v)$, regardless of which two vertices $u$ and $v$ are chosen or which specific fault set $F$ is considered. This framework is particularly relevant for graph classes with bounded treewidth, including planar graphs. Our work presents a $(2,3)$-dimensional distance labeling for planar graphs that is robust against the removal of any three vertices. Additionally, we demonstrate that our labeling can be constructed in $O(n)$ time, where $n$ denotes the graph's vertex count.

We investigate the time- and frequency-domain two-particle correlations of a driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard system. Beginning with an exact solution to the single-particle density matrix, we derive an efficient method to compute the full two-particle density matrix in real time. Subsequently, we determine the frequency-domain two-particle correlation functions by applying a Fourier transform. Our analysis reveals that in regimes of strong driving, these correlations exhibit peaks at frequencies corresponding to two-particle loss modes. Additionally, we observe a strong link between single-particle and two-particle correlations, demonstrating that the former can serve as a predictive tool for the latter.

Recent research has established that adversarial training can significantly enhance an neural network's robustness against attacks, primarily by modeling input data as probabilistic distributions and optimizing the lower bound of expected logarithmic likelihood. Building on this concept, we introduce a novel approach for identifying inputs that fall outside the training distribution. This is achieved by replacing standard convolutional layers with new components known as distributional Gaussian process (GP) layers capable of outputting Gaussian distributions. These specialized layers are trained using the aforementioned variational lower-bound objective, which inherently encourages the learned distributions to align with the training data. Consequently, during deployment, out-of-domain inputs are flagged if their corresponding layer distributions assign low probabilities. We demonstrate empirically that this method offers robust protection against a wide range of $l_2$-norm bounded attacks and achieves superior performance in detecting unknown input distributions compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Periodically driven isolated quantum systems can develop eigenstates that mimic the properties of the thermal ensemble, a phenomenon known as thermal-scarring. This study investigates how such states emerge in an experimentally feasible open and non-equilibrium system: a single site of a driven dissipative quantum circuit. Our analysis demonstrates that, within a specific parameter regime, the system's dynamics generate scar-like modes characterized by low heating. Consequently, this results in anomalous, circuit-temperature-independent ground-state occupancy of nearly all qubits. We further show that, in a particular dissipative Floquet-heating regime, the system's steady state resembles a BEC. This condensate is distinguished by non-Gaussian correlations and enhanced entanglement entropy relative to the circuit. These findings offer a new approach to engineering and observing scar states and non-equilibrium BECs in practical, open quantum systems.

This paper establishes a strengthened maximum principle for weak solutions of the Monge–Ampère equation. Furthermore, for such solutions $u$ on a convex domain $\Omega$, the following Hölder bound holds:

Time-domain analysis is a fundamental component of the experimental evaluation of modern optical atomic clocks. While current periodic-time characterization techniques are well-established, our work addresses time-dependent fluctuations in the operation of optical atomic clocks. We present a framework for analyzing these non-periodic clock fluctuations, involving the development of a classification method based on a new metric that distinguishes between stochastic and deterministic behaviors. We apply this classification to real-clock data and utilize it to investigate how environmental factors and operational parameters influence these non-periodic fluctuations. We anticipate that these findings will significantly enhance the future modeling and experimental analysis of time-dependent noise in cutting-edge timekeeping devices.

This paper introduces a novel real-time Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and fog computing framework designed to optimize Service Function Chaining (SVF) performance by dynamically balancing network resources. Our approach employs domain controllers to monitor end-to-end flows and maintain end-to-end Service Level Agreements (SLAs) by selecting fog nodes based on specific criteria, including VF instance count, CPU usage, and power consumption. To ensure flow processing reliability, controllers utilize a multi-objective optimization algorithm to generate resilient primary and backup forwarding rules. Furthermore, to mitigate faults and enhance performance, the system implements a proactive strategy that anticipates potential failures and establishes preventive measures. The effectiveness of this solution is validated through extensive simulations comparing it against current state-of-the-art techniques.

The choice of loss function is pivotal in training deep neural networks, yet the influence of its specific components remains poorly understood. We introduce an original methodology—gradient surgery—to analyze a function's influence during optimization by temporarily modifying it mid-training. Applying this technique to image classification, we demonstrate that gradient surgery offers clearer insights into loss dynamics than standard statistical measures computed on the full training set. Specifically, we reveal that conventional cross-entropy loss drives excessive focus on dominant classes, thereby hindering model robustness. Furthermore, the method facilitates the creation of novel loss functions by enabling targeted optimization of specific gradient properties.

We introduce the hyper-invariant MERA (HiMER A), a new approximate holographic error correction code. This code is constructed by applying a sequence of unitary transformations to a quantum state, where each unitary remains invariant under a specific group action. This invariance constraint significantly reduces the search space for unitaries, making the code both efficient and versatile. Additionally, the HiMER A functions as a quantum generalization of the hyperbolic Monge-Ampère space (HM), a classical framework previously utilized in holography. By analyzing the properties of this coding scheme, we demonstrate that HiMER A exhibits power-law correlations within a holographic dual description. We further provide an analytical derivation of the dual geometry, which is a hyperbolic generalization of the anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime known as Asymptotically Hyperbolic Manifold (AHM). In this geometric setting, the radial direction of the holographic surface corresponds to the degree of entanglement within the code. We also derive an expression for the entanglement entropy of HiMER A, which is determined by the entanglement entropy of the underlying HM state. Finally, we establish a connection between the entanglement entropy of the dual AHM and the entanglement negativity of the quantum code.

Galactic Center filaments are elongated, dense structures that dominate the region's appearance. This study investigates the spacing between them, revealing that the distance from one filament to the next follows a lognormal distribution. The observed average spacing is approximately 0.15 parsecs, which is notably smaller than the typical filament length of 0.4 parsecs. This finding suggests the need to refine current models of filament formation and evolution.

This study introduces a distributed strategy for implementing Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) across voltage levels in integrated primary-secondary distribution networks. The approach relies on iterative exchanges of limited data between neighboring secondary and primary buses to determine secondary-level CVR switches, while simultaneously coordinating with primary system equipment. The design is grounded in distributed optimization principles and operates by decomposing the problem into local and global components. The primary objective is to reduce specific node voltages to designated targets along primary lines without increasing losses, power flows, or violating any operational constraints. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through its application to the IEEE 123-bus distribution network, which incorporates an IEEE 37-bus secondary system.

We investigate nonstochastic bandits and scenarios with experts characterized by arm-specific delays, a setting where each arm's associated delay is assigned independently and identically distributed values drawn from an arbitrary distribution. In this context, selecting a specific arm results in a immediate regret cost for the player alongside a cumulative delay cost incurred by all arms that share that particular delay value. We demonstrate that a straightforward, index-based algorithm performs competitively within $\mathcal{O}(\log K)$ factors relative to both nonstochastic bandits and scenarios with experts, specifically regarding regret bound tightness. Furthermore, we establish an information-theoretic lower bound of $\mathcal{O}(\log K)$ for both fixed and time-varying delay distributions, which demonstrates that our algorithm's performance guarantees are optimal.

Dialogue systems are increasingly vital in real-world settings, yet a primary hurdle remains the tendency of current models to produce unnatural, repetitive, or nonsensical responses. This paper introduces a new learning framework called LEATHER (Learning to Emit A Human-like Emotional and Textually-Human Replies), which generates conversation turns that mimic human patterns more closely. Our approach relies on a generative model that imitates human similarity across two dimensions: semantic content and textual form. To achieve this, we leverage a large dataset of human-written Wikipedia dialogue pairs, where each entry represents a self-contained conversation thread. By training a model to predict the preceding turn within these pairs, we enable it to produce outputs that closely resemble actual human language. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method generates significantly more human-like text compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, we present a new evaluation metric that quantifies the "human-likeness" of automated dialogue more accurately than previous measures. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/robertgao/leather.

This article presents an overview of recent lattice QCD findings regarding systems at finite temperature and density, with a particular emphasis on the quark-meson phase transition occurring within the pure SU(3) gauge theory as a reference framework for investigating phase transitions in full QCD characterized by non-zero net baryon density.

The escalating demand for renewable energy has spurred the development of larger offshore wind turbines, which necessitates sophisticated numerical models for the early-stage design optimization of these systems. While computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations are standard for predicting aerodynamic and hydrodynamic forces on individual turbines, their high computational cost renders them unsuitable for modeling loads on full turbines or entire farms. To address this limitation, data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as a promising alternative. This study introduces a novel framework utilizing Gaussian processes (GP) to construct a probabilistic surrogate model capable of simulating aerodynamic and hydrodynamic loads on offshore wind turbines. By employing a chained architecture, the approach decomposes the simulation into two stages: first, a reduced-order model (ROM) generates probabilistic time series of key aerodynamic and hydrodynamic parameters, and second, GP-based regressors estimate the resulting loads based on these reduced-order outputs. The model's validity is verified against data from a benchmark simulation of an offshore wind turbine interacting with a passing wave group. Results indicate that this strategy effectively captures load statistics, offering a highly efficient and computationally tractable method for integrating into early design optimization workflows.

Natural disasters can be effectively analyzed through social media, which offers real-time data on affected regions. This study examines the Twitter response to the May 2020 earthquake in Izmir, Turkey. The analysis, conducted on Twitter data collected during and immediately following the event, utilizes both network and topic modeling to assess social media activity. Specifically, social network analysis explores the structural characteristics of the resulting network, while topic modeling identifies prevalent themes within the tweets. Findings indicate that the network is small-world, scale-free, and highly centralized, with retweets dominating user interactions. Furthermore, the research distinguishes between the tweet content based on the account type, revealing that while the networks within real-time accounts share similar structures to those in retweeters, the latter dominate overall. Finally, the analysis of these accounts uncovers distinct differences in topics between real-time accounts and retweeters.

The $R_\infty$ property characterizes spaces with infinite rational homotopy type, specifically referring to groups that admit infinite conjugacy classes under reversal of words. In this work, we investigate whether such a property holds for the nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Houghton groups. Our investigation demonstrates that these groups do not possess the $R_\infty$ property when the groups are generalized solvable Baumb-Solitar groups of height 2 and 3, specifically when acting on the integers via affine transformations of rank 1 modulo higher dimensions. Our argument relies on the construction of specific elements in the groups that are invariant under conjugation by powers of generators, and this construction is of particular importance for the derivation of our results.

We introduce a forward-optimization approach to invert time-resolved data within a trajectory basis, a method that yields robust results, particularly when input data contains noise. This technique avoids reliance on specific trajectory properties, such as their completeness or the absence of outliers, and instead focuses on identifying a trajectory that is robustly consistent with the experimental data. This optimizer is applied to invert time-resolved spectroscopic data, such as time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XANES) and time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-PE). Specifically, an experimental TR-XANES dataset from a CuO$_2$ plane in a CuO$_2$ plane is analyzed, and the results are discussed in relation to the presence of charge ordering in the system. This work demonstrates the potential of this method to extract reliable dynamical information from complex experimental data.

We introduce a forward-optimization approach to invert time-resolved data within a trajectory basis, a method that yields robust results, particularly when input data contains noise. This technique avoids reliance on specific trajectory properties, such as their completeness or the absence of outliers, and instead focuses on identifying a trajectory that is robustly consistent with the experimental data. This optimizer is applied to invert time-resolved spectroscopic data, such as time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XANES) and time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-PE). This paper introduces SceNDD, a naturalistic driving dataset focused on scenarios. We detail the data collection methodology, the annotation specifications, and the evaluation metrics. To validate these, we developed several scenario-based approaches, including scenario completion, scenario prediction, and scenario retrieval. Additionally, we established fundamental scenarios, such as lane changes, to serve as benchmarks for comparison. To our knowledge, this is the first study to employ such a comprehensive dataset and these specific driving tasks.

We demonstrate that a boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) can be represented as a conformal field theory on an internal interface within a higher-dimensional space, a construction termed Internal Interface Decomposition (IID). This representation enables a novel calculation of the reflected entropy for the boundary setup. Specifically, the reflected entropy corresponds to that of the internal interface, which can be evaluated via the modular $S$-matrix derived from a relevant bulk effective field theory. This approach facilitates the analytical computation of reflected entropy in specific IID models, such as the Ising model with a boundary, and allows for the determination of the monophilar entropy channel capacity in IID boundary theories mapped to a 1+1-dimensional internal interface.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology to boost spectral efficiency in 6G systems. However, channel estimation in RIS-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) environments remains difficult due to a high dimensionality channel matrix, often exacerbated by the use of insufficient Cyclic Prefix (CP) and hardware imperfections. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an Enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) based channel estimator. This approach is designed to be more accurate and computationally efficient than traditional methods. The proposed estimator is evaluated under realistic conditions, specifically considering an incomplete CP structure and impairments such as gain mismatch and phase errors. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed ELM-based method significantly outperforms conventional techniques in the presence of these combined challenges.

We demonstrate that the average logarithm of the logarithm of the probability distribution of energy measurements, divided by the inverse of the number of measurements, converges to a value that is less than or equal to the logarithm of the probability distribution of energy measurements, divided by the inverse of the number of measurements. This value is strictly less than the logarithm of the probability distribution of energy measurements, divided by the inverse of the number of measurements. This extension holds true for arbitrary initial states and measurement operations, regardless of projectivity. We examine the deformation theory of instantons associated with the group G2. The linearized deforming differential operator for G-instantons, when the underlying geometry is nearly G2-symmetric, is elliptic; this result allows us to demonstrate that locally, the moduli space of G2-instantons possesses a smooth structure. The findings are further generalized to nearly G2-symmetric 7-manifolds, where we analyze and describe the obstruction space governing deformations of G2-instantons.

The widespread adoption of contact tracing applications has sparked significant debate regarding their privacy implications. This paper addresses that concern by constructing a comprehensive, unified framework that integrates the standard SIR epidemiological model with a "random walk" model for user movement. We introduce the "Random Walk Susceptible-Infected-Recovered" (RWSIR) model, which accounts for privacy risks by incorporating the probabilistic behavior of app users. We demonstrate that the long-term infection prevalence is independent of initial conditions and derive a closed-form expression for the basic reproduction number, $R_0$. Furthermore, we establish that the steady-state infection prevalence is a non-increasing function of the probability that users report their contacts. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, increasing the likelihood of contact reporting can inadvertently boost the overall recovery rate. Additionally, we observe that as the probability of contact reporting approaches zero, the system's steady-state state converges to the classic SIR equilibrium.

This short review explores the potential role of quantum information in biological neural systems, beginning with a brief overview of the mechanisms proposed in the literature for quantum coherence within neurons. It then outlines the current theoretical models regarding DNA and other molecular structures as possible media for quantum information processing. Finally, the article examines the challenges associated with monitoring quantum effects in living systems and discusses future experimental strategies for such detection.

This work presents a code generator built in ACL2 capable of producing formal proofs for properties concerning C programs. It employs a shallow embedding approach, defining C constructs directly using ACL2 Shallow Embedding rules. The framework includes a code generator that not only translates C programs into ACL2 representations but also automatically constructs proofs for specified properties. Demonstrations are provided for programs involving arithmetic operations, arborescent data structures, and mutual recursion.

Ramanujan proposed a conjectured formula expressing odd zeta values. Subsequent research by Broadhurst provided both evidence and generalizations supporting this Ramanujan formula. In the present study, we employ the Furusawa-Berger-Broderick approach utilizing Hurwitz zeta functions to establish the original Ramanujan conjecture. Furthermore, we apply our methodology to derive additional formulas analogous to Ramanujan's identity.

We derive the $S^1$-equivariant elliptic cohomology groups for complex projective spaces $\text{CP}(V)$, where $V$ is a finite-dimensional complex vector space, under the standard linear $S^1$-action. Additionally, we demonstrate how our derived formula can be utilized to reconstruct the Witten genus of certain holomorphic torus bundles over CP$(V)$.

This study explores the utility of machine learning within algebraic geometry for physics applications. We begin by outlining an approach to determine the complete set of equations defining a specific variety from a given dataset of its points. Next, we examine how these varieties can be represented as neural networks, enabling the application of back-propagation to solve inverse problems involving radiation-holographic dualities. Finally, we investigate the reconstruction of stability manifolds for the O(2) and observation of their fractal dimensions using this technique.

This research examines the total cross sections and angular distributions of $J/\psi$ arising from the $e^+e^- \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) processes at next-to-leading order (NLO) within QCD framework, utilizing center-of-mass energies near 10.58 GeV. Our NLO analysis demonstrates that radiative corrections are substantial, reaching approximately 30% to 40% for total cross sections. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of virtual-light parton (VLP) contributions on these distributions. Our findings indicate that these NLO corrections and the associated angular distributions are expected to be measured by the BESIII experiment.

This paper investigates how casual Signal enthusiasts and casual users comprehend PINs. We conducted interviews with 16 participants, asking them to configure their PINs and explaining their reasoning. Our findings reveal that users tend to select PINs based on their personal significance rather than security, leading them to misunderstand how Signal PINs function. Consequently, users may believe their messages are accessible to others despite the PINs being compromised. We conclude by offering recommendations for future research and Signal updates to address these misconceptions.
This technical brief details the generation of Gaussian quadrature formulas to precisely and effectively solve for the net area under the solar radiation curve, regardless of time of day or season.

Relying on the geodesic normal coordinate system, Riemannian optimization seeks to navigate tangent spaces to reach local minima. A key challenge in this approach is determining the search path within the tangent space, which is achieved by solving optimization problems using the Gauss-Newton (GN) approximation. However, when dealing with high-dimensional inputs, the inherent rank of this GN matrix often exceeds the input size, creating a computational bottleneck. To resolve this, we introduce a new representation termed ViViT (Visualizing and Interpreting the tangent space via Low-rank Tangents), which captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of the GN matrix. By approximating this structure, we transform the original optimization problem into a much more efficient formulation. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting error from this approximation is negligible. Empirical results further demonstrate that ViViT achieves performance on par with the state-of-the-art while delivering substantial improvements in speed.

In natural language, gender-marking systems assign each noun a specific grammatical gender, such as masculine, feminine, or neuter. These systems are believed to originate from a historical process where a language's original single concept of male-centric "people" bifurcated into distinct male and non male (or female/neuter) categories. Consequently, this raises the question of whether modern grammatical gender still influences how humans mentally represent these concepts. To address this, we analyzed existing evidence and conducted a large-scale study using multilingual BERT models. Our work demonstrates that these powerful transformer-based models successfully capture noun representations aligned with grammatical gender in male and female/neuter categories. Furthermore, we found that both real human data and the artificial patterns detected by the models provide strong support for the hypothesis that grammatical gender shapes noun representations.

This study examines two concepts: the chimamenability of a topological space and its stiffness. A space is defined as charmenable if it admits a free action by a discrete group such that the quotient space remains homotopy equivalent to the original. Conversely, a space is stiff when every discrete group acting freely on it does so with an infinite center. This note demonstrates that for any arithmetic lattice within a simple Lie group, its normalizer constitutes a charmable group, and specifically, its center is infinite. Consequently, we establish that all arithmetic lattices in simple Lie groups are stiff.

Object pose estimation is a critical component of many robotic vision tasks. While existing methods are typically category-level, they necessitate training data for specific object categories, which restricts their practical application. This paper introduces a zero-shot approach that eliminates the training requirement for new object categories. By leveraging large-scale datasets, we learn to predict the relative pose of objects within their 3D bounding boxes. This relative pose is subsequently combined with the 3D bounding boxes predicted by a pre-trained detector to recover the full 6DoF pose. We also present a new training strategy for 3D bounding box detection that significantly enhances the accuracy of this proposed method. Extensive experiments on the Pascal-Context and ScanNetv2 datasets demonstrate that our approach can accurately estimate the pose of previously unseen categories without any training.

Accurately forecasting traffic conditions is vital for urban planning and traffic management. However, conventional methods often fail to account for traffic data's unique characteristics, specifically its sparsity and massive scale. This paper introduces a novel approach to traffic forecasting that leverages data similarity. We first identify traffic patterns that are similar to the target pattern and subsequently utilize these related scenarios to enhance forecasting performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we validate that our approach remains robust even when dealing with sparse data and massive traffic volumes.

Causal inference is a method for deducing cause-and-effect relationships from data, enabling the prediction of outcomes resulting from hypothetical interventions or counterfactual scenarios. Causal Graphical Models (CGMs) represent causal relationships using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where nodes signify variables and arrows denote direct causal effects. While learning CGMs from data is challenging, it is a critical first step toward causal inference. This study introduces VACA, a novel Variational approach to learning these models specifically for intervention and counterfactual queries. VACA employs a variational autoencoder framework to learn a latent representation of the CGM, which subsequently facilitates inference. By utilizing variational inference, the approach can learn CGMs from a single dataset, thereby eliminating the need for separate datasets to distinguish between observational and interventional data. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that VACA effectively recovers the true causal graph structure and accurately forecasts the distribution under intervention or counterfactual conditions.

Real-time transient acquisition (REALTA) is a backend system that operates within the I-LovAR LOFAR observatory's I-LovAR station. It is designed to process data in real time to detect transient radio signals. This paper presents initial findings from REALTA's deployment at ILOVAV's ILOVAV site. We describe the system's architecture, software, and data processing pipelines, then show that REALTA successfully identified numerous transients, including fast radio bursts (FRBs), by analyzing data from ILOVAV's ILOVAV station. We also compare REALTA's performance with that of traditional LOFAR data analysis pipelines, finding that REALTA achieves a detection rate that surpasses traditional methods by a factor of X while reducing false positives by a factor of Y. We conclude that REALTA is a promising tool for detecting transients in real time and suggest that it will be an important component of future radio astronomy observatories.

The advent of machine learning has triggered a paradigm shift across numerous scientific disciplines, including metaphotonics. Metaphotonics is a burgeoning field dedicated to investigating the fundamental principles governing the light-matter interaction within evanescent waves. This text reviews current research where machine learning is applied to investigate and optimize light-matter dynamics in the metastaphotonic domain. It begins by outlining the foundational concepts of metaphotonics and machine learning, followed by an exploration of how these techniques are utilized to deduce and streamline light-matter behavior. Furthermore, the paper examines emerging research directions and the transformative potential of metaphotonics when enhanced by artificial intelligence.

This paper introduces a comprehensive, expanded, and current dataset containing over 1.2 million movies from 2000 to 2020. This resource surpasses prior studies in terms of both dataset size and temporal scope. We utilize this dataset to examine how various pre-release attributes influence box office revenue. By applying a regression analysis approach, we assess the impact of diverse features—including genre, director, cast, and production company—on gross revenue. Our findings reveal that while certain attributes significantly affect revenue outcomes, others do not exhibit a statistically meaningful influence.

This research investigates the impact of secondary frequency control on voltage and frequency behaviors within power systems. The analysis relies on a time-scale separation model, which assumes slow secondary control acting upon fast primary regulation, fast network dynamics, and load variations. Under the framework of linear time-invariant models, we derive closed-form analytical conditions for the stability of eigenvalues. Our findings indicate that activating secondary frequency control can significantly enhance both frequency and voltage system stability. Furthermore, the study examines how secondary control parameters interact with other elements of the power system and assesses their sensitivity. Ultimately, the work aims to clarify frequency and voltage dynamics mechanisms, offering a conceptual basis for future research and the development of comprehensive control strategies.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are increasingly becoming "systems of systems" (SoS), characterized by the convergence of physical and virtual infrastructures, the dynamic interaction between them, and the capability to adapt to evolving operational contexts. As these complex CPS-SoS architectures grow in scale and complexity, the challenge of managing their dynamic environments and ensuring the delivery of essential services has intensified. Addressing these hurdles necessitates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) to bolster cyber-physical systems with inherent intelligence. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of AI techniques designed to empower cyber-physical CPS-SoS, specifically focusing on machine learning and deep learning approaches. These methods are essential for enhancing decision-making capabilities, optimizing resource allocation, and ensuring reliable service provision within these sophisticated cyber-physical systems.

This paper investigates the hypothesis that UV and soft X-ray excesses in blazar spectra originate from radiation produced by partially polarized incident light fields interacting with relativistic electrons. We employ a novel Monte-Carlo code, MAPPIES, to analyze spectral energy distributions of selected Fermi-LAT BL Lacs. By comparing these synthetic spectra with observed data, we determine the most probable ranges for key physical parameters, specifically the degree of incident polarization and the distribution of incident photon angles relative to the jet axis. Our findings indicate that a radiation mechanism driven by highly polarized, obliquely incident photons offers a viable explanation for the soft X-ray/UV excesses in BL Lacs.

We introduce a universal framework for analyzing complex landscapes, featuring an energy-dependent local resolution that improves as resolution decreases with lower energy. Within this setup, the local density of states adheres to a universal scaling law, and the local density of states' spatial distribution follows a universal scaling function. These findings are validated in the study of a many-body localized (MBL) spin chain, a system previously shown to develop glassy characteristics at both single-particle and few-particle energy scales. Specifically, the emergence of analytic continuation from eigenstates to the corresponding generalized coherent states is demonstrated.

We introduce an online method for identifying unknown symmetric states within the online quantum learning framework. This approach is evaluated using the success probability of accurately determining the target state after observing online data. Our findings indicate that the success probability approaches one as the number of observations increases, without requiring the prior knowledge of optimal measurement strategies or the count of observation samples needed for accuracy. Consequently, this represents the first online quantum learning method that achieves an asymptotically optimal sample complexity.

Baryon production is analyzed within the QCD string quantized fragmentation model, which incorporates helical string configurations. These configurations are favored for strings exhibiting a pronounced effective angular momentum. The analysis reveals that the string's tilt angle is the primary determinant of the generated baryon-to-meson ratio. The findings align with the predictions of the Lund string model, which also accounts for significant angular momentum, while simultaneously offering a more favorable explanation for the substantial baryon-to-meson ratio observed in ultra-peripheral proton–lead collisions.

The Sun's continuous surface flows generate magnetic active regions, which are traditionally identified by their extreme local velocities. However, recent findings indicate that the Sun's global meridional circulation is significantly altered by flows in the vicinity of these regions. This study investigates how such active region flows impact helioseismic travel-time measurements across the entire disk, specifically examining their influence on north-south travel-time data used to determine the global circulation pattern. We model the Sun as a sphere with a background flow component and superimpose synthetic active regions, utilizing a travel-time algorithm based on the oscillatory Green's function of the wave equation. Our results show that a single active region can induce travel-time variations of up to 0.05 ms, with the primary effect arising from the large-scale flow surrounding the region rather than magnetic effects within it. These perturbations exhibit a strong dependence on spot size, peaking at approximately 1.5 Mm in diameter. When a typical distribution of active regions is added to a global meridional circulation scenario, the resulting travel-time variations are analyzed. We conclude that a global circulation of 20 m s$^{-1}$ can be masked by an active region distribution peaking at 1.5 Mm in diameter and occurring every 15 days. This masking effect is most pronounced in the outer 10 degrees near the surface, where active region velocities are highest. Consequently, these findings suggest that future helioseismic determinations of global circulation must account for

We investigate the spectrum of stochastic gravitational waves generated by magnetic fields existing in the primordial universe. Our analysis indicates that even if primordial magnetic fields are orders of magnitude below the critical density ($B \sim 10^{-14} g/cm^3$), PTA arrays could still detect the associated background signals. Specifically, such fields would create a distinct upward curvature in the strain spectrum at frequencies below $10^{-9}$ Hz, potentially allowing current PTA observations to place meaningful constraints on primordial magnetic intensity.

Light field technology has gained significant traction in recent years due to its capacity to capture both spatial and angular viewpoints. However, this dual capability results in high-dimensional data that poses significant challenges for image compression. To address this, we introduce a disparity-aware model that employs learning-based techniques to compress light field images. Central to our approach is the construction of disparity maps, which serve as the foundation for generating disparity-aware kernels. These specialized kernels are utilized within a disparity-aware residual decoder to facilitate image reconstruction. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art compressions for light field images.

This study investigates the utility of combining advantages from both interactive and non-interactive models within vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (V-IR). We demonstrate through extensive experiments that incorporating a non-interactive component into a neural interactive model significantly boosts V-IR performance. To achieve this, we introduce a new framework called "Hybrid Query Expansion" (HQE), which expands queries by applying traditional query expansion techniques to the expanded input of a neural interactive model. Our findings indicate that HQE surpasses current state-of-the-art interactive approaches in V-IR tasks. Additionally, we present a new HQE model architecture that further improves retrieval results by synergizing the strengths of both non-interactive and interactive systems.

This paper evaluates the design-based and model-based design- and model-based approaches to small-area estimation in low-and middle-income countries. Using data from the 2016/2017 Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) for Uganda, we employed a linear mixed model incorporating covariates and random DHS cluster effects to estimate maternal and child mortality rates. Our analysis compared three methods: the design-based approach, a linear mixed model, and DHS-complex linear mixed model. We found that the design-based method produced more accurate estimates than the linear mixed model, while a complex linear mixed model that incorporated design features performed best. This study investigates repeated betting on the outcomes of a binary system modeled by a pair of non-orthogonal pure quantum states, $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$. We examine the optimal strategy for maximizing the betting capital over time, which grows exponentially at rates determined by the quantum payoff, a variant of the classical payoff defined in reference [1]. We further explore the asymptotic behavior of the logarithm of the maximum capital across a broad range of scenarios, analyzing the results through a continuous variable framework. We also discuss connections to quantum hypothesis testing and outline potential extensions to cases involving more than two states.

This study investigates the quasiparticle band alignment and optical excitonic properties of two-dimensional MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials (M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As) utilizing first-principles calculations. We demonstrate that these materials exhibit either type-II staggered or type-I straight band alignments when paired with h-BN or MoS$_2$. The type-II configuration fosters spatial separation between electron-hole pairs, thereby promoting efficient exciton dissociation into charge carriers, whereas the type-1 arrangement is conducive to forming bound excitonic states. Notably, the binding energies of these excitons significantly surpass those of common van der Waals materials like h-BN and WS$_2$. Crucially, binding energies remain unaffected by stacking order or twist angle, indicating that stacking variations do not influence excitonic stability. Additionally, the substantial Rashba spin-orbit coupling constant suggests these compounds are well-suited for spintronic applications.

This paper presents an investigation into the decay process $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, utilizing data from $1.8\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV collected by the LHCb detector. The analysis focuses on the invariant mass spectrum of the dimuon pair, observing no significant signal above the background in the relevant mass range. Consequently, the study establishes the most stringent upper limits to date on the branching fraction for this transition, which is less than $1.2 \times 10^{-9}$ at the 90% confidence level.

The formation of planetary systems begins with the collapse of a prestellar core. We have employed 3D smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations to track the evolution of protoplanetary disk formation, utilizing the gravitational potential of an embedded star as a key constraint. We compared the outcomes against the widely accepted passive, viscous, and tilted disk models. Our findings indicate that disks form rapidly, within approximately 10,000 years, and that their properties are significantly dictated by the core's initial angular momentum and the mass accretion rate from the star. We also observed a strong correlation between the star's spin and the disk's inclination, a relationship consistent with predictions from the tilted disk model. Finally, we note that the gas in these disks possesses substantial angular momentum, raising questions regarding the mechanisms responsible for angular momentum loss necessary for gas to eventually accrete onto the star.

Atmospheric dispersion (AD) significantly impacts both the quality and stability of astronomical imagery. Although AD correction is standard practice, its precise characterization remains difficult, often leading to unaccounted residuals that degrade data. This study presents a new method for measuring AD, implemented via a correction algorithm that utilizes on-sky observations of point sources. By analyzing the spatial distortion introduced by AD, the algorithm estimates the atmospheric dispersion profile (ADP) and atmospheric refraction profile (ARDP) with a precision of 0.001 arcsec, a level of accuracy that surpasses current standards. These high-fidelity profiles were validated using measurements taken at the ESO La Silla 2.6-meter telescope, covering a range of zenith angles from 30° to 65° and observing wavelengths from 4000 to 10,000 Angstroms. The results demonstrate that the estimated ADP and ARDP align closely with theoretical models, with discrepancies remaining below 0.001 arcsec.

This study addresses the challenge of multi-period time series forecasting, which involves predicting a series of outputs for a single input sequence. This scenario is prevalent in fields like healthcare and finance, where, for instance, a single diagnostic test yields a set of results or one financial indicator predicts multiple future metrics. Although existing time series models can predict these outcomes, they typically fail to incorporate the dependencies between the different variables. To tackle this, we introduce a novel Bayesian time series model that utilizes a latent variable to capture these inter-correlations, thereby enabling more accurate predictions. Furthermore, we implement a variational inference algorithm to facilitate efficient, scalable parameter estimation. To prevent overfitting and enhance interpretability, we integrate a sparsity-inducing prior directly into the model. We validate our approach on both synthetic data and real-world financial records, demonstrating that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in predictive accuracy.

This paper examines fairness and privacy within Federated Learning (FL) environments, focusing on scenarios where clients possess varying amounts of sensitive data. We introduce a novel fairness metric for Federated Learning and develop a new federated differential privacy (FDP) framework. Our approach ensures that clients with less data are not disadvantaged, thereby promoting equitable learning outcomes while protecting individual privacy.

We introduce a supersymmetric extension of the standard model featuring an additional $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, motivated by the concept of a universal extra dimension. In this framework, every standard model field possesses a corresponding partner in the bulk, while a right-handed fermion in the bulk—specifically the $\chi$ field—remains single. This structure results in an extra $U(1)_X$ factor within the four-dimensional effective theory. The model's renormalizability is established, and it is demonstrated that supersymmetry breaking can occur via the $\chi F$ term. We analyze the radiative corrections to muon and b-muon decays, the resulting supersymmetric particle mass spectra, and determine viable parameter spaces that allow the right-handed $\nu_{\chi}$ fermion to serve as a viable dark matter candidate.

This study investigates a wireless network powered by radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting, equipped with an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). In this setup, an RF source (RS) emits energy to an IRS, which redirects the signal toward an RF energy transfer (RFT) device (RFT-D); subsequently, the RFT-D transmits data to a base station (BS) using the harvested energy. The primary objective is to jointly optimize the IRS configuration and the RFT-D's transmit power to maximize system throughput. Due to the non-convex nature of this problem, we introduce a deep unsupervised learning (DUL) framework capable of generating high-throughput configurations. Specifically, we construct a generative adversarial network (GAN) where the generator creates feasible reflection phase shifts and the discriminator estimates the corresponding system throughput. To mitigate sample inefficiency inherent in training GANs, we employ a self-supervised learning strategy. Experimental results confirm that this proposed method outperforms existing algorithms in terms of throughput.

This study examines the delayed-neutron emission following the $\beta$-decay of $^{186}$Hg, a process critical for understanding nuclear structure and relevant to astrophysical phenomena. Utilizing the Advanced NSCL NS-2 magnetic spectrometer, researchers measured the absolute yield of these neutrons alongside their time distribution. The findings reveal an average delayed-neutron branching ratio of $P_{n}=0.015\pm0.003$. This value is notably lower than predictions from both macroscopic and microscopic-macroscopic models, as well as previous experimental data. The observed discrepancy is attributed to the fact that most $\beta$-decay $\beta$-strength populates single-particle states below the neutron separation energy, leaving few transitions capable of emitting additional neutrons.

We introduce a minimal extension to the Standard Model that simultaneously accounts for dark matter and explains the matter-antimatter asymmetry. This framework incorporates dark matter as a fermion that communicates with the visible sector exclusively through a Higgs boson, while the asymmetry arises from leptogenesis mediated by heavy right-handed neutrinos. These neutrinos couple both to the dark matter particle and to standard leptons. We analyze the constraints on their parameter space, specifically examining how their direct detection limits are modified by their interaction with dark matter. Furthermore, we explore scenarios where these interactions lead to resonant production of the heavy right-handed neutrinos, enabling the calculation of the resulting baryon asymmetry.

We introduce a learning-based control approach that integrates scarce data with sparse, high-level information to enhance learning efficiency. The core of this method is a "sketch-based" model predictive control (MPC) algorithm designed to handle complex dynamics by utilizing a data-driven model. This model is trained using the "System Identification with Sketched Features" (SISF) technique, which merges a few low-dimensional sketches with scarce data. The sketches are derived from the system's Lie algebra, enabling the model to capture the dynamics within an affine framework on the sketch space. The study demonstrates that this model achieves high accuracy with minimal data requirements. Furthermore, we present an offline strategy for generating these sketches, which relies on the system's integration trajectories. The proposed algorithm is validated through a control task involving a quadcopter navigating a three-dimensional environment.

We present a complete and explicit formulation of Ward identities within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This presentation is explicit for the identities linked to the simple Lie algebra currents and involves no currents associated with the Cartan currents. This formulation is achieved by applying a specific basis transformation to a previously established, general, but non-explicit form provided in an earlier study.

Relational graphs offer a powerful framework for representing structured data, where nodes signify entities and edges denote relationships. While graph convolutional networks have proven effective for node classification tasks, applying GANs to learn representations within structured data has historically been challenging. This work introduces a relational GAN (RGAN) designed to generate meaningful node and edge embeddings. The model leverages the triplet loss function to assess the realism of synthetic data against real samples, optimizing the learned feature distributions. Furthermore, we propose an extension incorporating node classification labels into the training process. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in node classification accuracy.

Twin-field quantum key distribution (TFQKD) is a keyless cryptographic protocol that achieves scaling efficiency of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$ relative to the total number of transmitted pulses, $N$. In contrast, standard QKD methods are limited to $\mathcal{O}(N)$ scaling. However, the initial version of TFQKD necessitated a phase-locking mechanism between laser sources, a requirement that introduces significant experimental complexity and restricts the protocol's broad applicability. This paper introduces a novel TFQKD variant that eliminates the need for phase locking. By employing an interference-free method to measure the differential phase, this new protocol maintains the favorable $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})}$ scaling while offering enhanced practicality and greater flexibility for real-world quantum communication applications.

The analysis provides explicit descriptions for both algebras, revealing that they are generated by the remaining projections alongside certain unitaries. The architecture of object detectors has advanced significantly in recent years, yet their reliance on specific classes remains a critical limitation. To address this, open and generalization object detection aim to detect both known and previously unseen categories. This research introduces a novel framework leveraging pseudo bounding-box labels to achieve high performance with minimal reliance on annotated data. By learning the inherent structures of bounding-box distributions, the model generates these synthetic labels for training. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks, including PASCAL VOC, COCO, and the dataset containing eleven novel categories.

This study investigates the distribution of ionized, PDR, and atomic gas surrounding the Class I protostar S1 within Rho Ophiuchus using CO+ (ionized), CO (PDR), and CS (atomic) emission data. We find that the ionized region extends to a radius of 0.04 pc, while the PDR region spans 0.04 to 0.12 pc. The CO emission from the PDR region is best modeled by a power-law profile with an index of -1.2, whereas the atomic gas follows a similar pattern with an index of -1.4. Furthermore, the observed power-law distributions align with predictions from hydrodynamical models of PDRs, which anticipate a CO power-law index between -1 and -2 for optically thin gas. The atomic gas distribution resembles a power law with a steeper gradient than that of CO, indicating a stronger concentration toward the PDR boundary. Additionally, the atomic gas appears to be heated by the protostar's outflow, as evidenced by the presence of a cavity in the distribution at approximately 0.1 pc. These findings offer critical insights into the interaction between protostellar outflows and surrounding interstellar medium.

Transformer architectures, which utilize self-attention mechanisms to model global contextual relationships, have achieved remarkable advancements in natural language processing (NLP). Conversely, their adoption within computer vision (CV) remains relatively recent. This paper presents a thorough survey of transformer applications in CV, covering various sub-fields including image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, video analysis, and three-dimensional computer vision. We also examine critical implementation challenges and current research trends, concluding with an overview of open research avenues for future work.

This study investigates time-variant factor loadings within factor models for forecasting mortality rates, utilizing a comparative analysis of death records from Sweden, the United States, and the United Kingdom spanning 1950 to 2020. The findings indicate that although both time-variant and time-variant models perform similarly in in-sample fit, the time-variant approach yields superior out-of-sample forecast accuracy. Furthermore, this model structure allows for the isolation of time-variant effects, offering valuable insights into shifts in mortality patterns.

This study addresses the prevalent issue of landscape interference in neural architecture search (NAS), where suboptimal architectures discovered in earlier trials hinder subsequent searches. Such interference not only degrades the quality of final outputs but also significantly increases computational costs due to repeated exploration of previously failed areas. We introduce a theoretical framework to characterize interference and outline a strategy to detect and mitigate it. Our approach employs a lightweight sub-search to identify high-performance architectures, allowing the primary NAS process to bypass the investigation of inferior candidates. Empirical evaluations on various deep learning benchmarks, including those for image classification and language modeling, demonstrate that our method substantially enhances both the quality and efficiency of the architecture search.

Time series data is prevalent across numerous scientific domains, characterized by the necessity to track the evolution of a specific phenomenon over an extended period. Analyzing these data sets is particularly challenging due to their high dimensionality, inherent noise, and complex dependencies. To address these issues, the field of time series analysis has developed various methodologies for extracting meaningful insights. This paper introduces an R package named `time_series_features` (referred to in the source as `theft`, aligning with the original text) that offers functions for generating time series features. By leveraging these tools, users can perform dimensionality reduction, effectively manage noise, and model dependencies within their data sets. Furthermore, the author provides examples of applications for these features in predicting and classifying tasks.

The growing prominence of machine translation has intensified the need for human post-editing. As professional translators perform this editing, they often work on numerous projects across diverse domains, such as legal texts or scientific articles. Determining which projects a translator can successfully translate serves as a critical factor for both the translator and the translation service provider. This study introduces a Bayesian framework to evaluate a translator's reliability within specific domains, offering a more nuanced insight into their capabilities than a simple proficiency rating. The findings demonstrate that this Bayesian approach yields more dependable outcomes than the Maximum Likelihood Estimation method. Furthermore, the research highlights the significant impact of dataset size on the precision of reliability assessments.

Using principles from supersymmetric quantum mechanics, we establish sum rules for the complex eigenvalues of channels in scattering systems, a finding applicable broadly to complex many-body systems. These eigenvalues correspond to the "eigenstates" of channels, a concept central to understanding their dynamics. The first sum rule constrains the algebraic sum of real eigenvalues, while the second addresses the disparity between the largest and minimal real parts within a complex channel set. The derived rules are particularly effective for analyzing scenarios where complex eigenvalues are tightly clustered. The study also establishes upper bounds for complex phase deviations from their respective values. The significance of these theoretical predictions is validated through numerical tests on both analytically solvable models and complex computational simulations.

Pruning has emerged as a powerful technique for compressing deep neural networks, yet a significant challenge remains: identifying which specific features to prune. Current methods predominantly rely on heuristics, such as the magnitude of weights or feature map activations, to sift through feature networks. However, these heuristics fail to account for the non-Gaussian distribution of activation statistics, which are critical for understanding the relationships between layers. This work introduces a novel, principled approach to pruning convolutional networks, tailored to the specific statistical profiles of these networks. We validate this approach on the ImageNet dataset, demonstrating that our method achieves superior accuracy and a greater compression rate compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a class of lottery games defined by a prize fund, an allocation strategy, and a ticket price. We demonstrate that the maximum expected profit for a lottery operator is reached when the prize fund is kept constant and distributed uniformly across all tickets. Under this optimal strategy, the expected value of each lottery ticket is determined by the ratio of the prize fund to the total number of tickets. Furthermore, we prove that an investor achieves their highest expected value by purchasing a single ticket when the cumulative amount spent remains fixed.

This result holds for arbitrary integer $Q$ and $N$. Additionally, our calculations confirm the $Q=1$ case through an independent direct computation.

While the distinct electronic valleys in two-dimensional materials have long been recognized for their significance in spintronics and computing, their potential for valley-specific phonon interactions remains underexplored. This study reveals that phonons can selectively modulate the electronic valley structure in certain two-dimensional systems, a phenomenon absent in conventional three-dimensional bulk materials. Specifically, we demonstrate that an unconventional deformation potential mechanism, arising from phonon-induced orbital mixing, can effectively open or close valley gaps. Furthermore, we illustrate how these effects manifest in transport properties, highlighting their potential for controlling valley Hall currents. These findings underscore the capacity of phonons to manipulate valley degrees of freedom in two-dimensional materials, establishing a foundation for future advancements in valley-based electronics.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a prevalent technique for visualizing high-dimensional datasets, yet it is constrained to mapping points onto a Euclidean space. This limitation is problematic for data that is inherently spherical, such as vectors situated on a hypersphere, where the geometric constraints of a flat space can hinder accurate analysis. To overcome this, we introduce Spherical Euclidean Neural Neighbor Embedding (SE-NNE), an algorithm designed to project spherical data into a lower-dimensional manifold while maintaining a null-sum constraint. We demonstrate that SE-NNE is mathematically equivalent to finding fixed points of certain smooth functions, which enables the derivation of various efficient iterative solvers. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical link between t-SNE and SE-NNE, showing that SE-NNE can be interpreted as a constrained, projected variant of the original t-SNE framework. Comprehensive experiments on both synthetic data and real-world applications confirm that SE-NNE produces embeddings that are more accurate than standard t-SNE for spherical datasets.

We investigate the fermionic polaron within two dimensions, specifically examining the correction to the quasiparticle residue and the effective mass arising from antiferromagnetic coupling between the polaron and a scattered impurity. Our implementation of a Diagram Monte Carlo method allows us to sum an extensive collection of self-energy contributions up to twenty-four terms. Our findings indicate that while the polaron behaves as a stable dressed quasiparticle, it may undergo a phase transition into a bound state when the coupling strength becomes sufficiently large.

This study introduces a hybrid analog-digital scheme utilizing the QFT-QMC method to simulate band insulators and superconductors. Leveraging the fact that fermionic wavefunctions can be efficiently represented via the fermionic path integral (FPI) framework, we split the FPI into two components: a fermionic term simulated using a digital algorithm and an bosonic term (representing the environment) handled through an analog approach. We evaluate the precision required for the digital segment to achieve thermodynamic quantities of sufficient accuracy. Our results indicate that for a 2D square lattice with one orbital per site, roughly 10 to 15 quantum gates per qubit are needed to precisely determine the ground state energy density of the coupled system. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of performing these calculations using adiabatic quantum computing.

Graph polynomials serve as valuable tools for characterizing various properties of graphs. This paper examines a sequence of polynomials, denoted $f_n(x)$, which connects to different graph invariants. Specifically, we establish connections between this sequence and well-known variants like the chromatic polynomial, the matching polynomial, and the generating function for the independence polynomial. Furthermore, we analyze fundamental characteristics of the sequence itself, demonstrating that for any non-negative integer $n$, $f_n(x)$ is real-rooted, and we derive bounds regarding its leading and trailing coefficients.
